cards.title: Kitchen oil fires
facts: Water on burning oil turns instantly to steam and throws burning oil into the air (a fireball).
Fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen. Covering the pan cuts off oxygen.
A covered pan should stay covered until it has completely cooled.
do: Turn off the stove or gas if you can reach it safely
Slide a metal lid or baking tray over the pan
Use a damp (wrung-out) towel if there is no lid
Get everyone out, close the kitchen door and call 101 or 112 if the fire spreads
dont: Never pour water on burning oil
Don't carry the burning pan outside
Don't throw flour on it, it can flare up

myths.statement: Water can put out any kind of fire.
myths.truth: Water makes oil and electrical fires much worse. Smother oil fires, and cut the power for electrical ones.

myths.statement: Covering a burning pan with a metal lid can put the fire out.
myths.truth: A lid cuts off oxygen. Keep it on until the pan cools down.

quiz.q: Oil in a pan catches fire. What's the safest first move?
options: Cover it with a metal lid
quiz.explanation: A lid cuts off oxygen. Water causes a dangerous fireball.

quiz.q: After covering a burning pan, when can you lift the lid?
options: Only when the pan has fully cooled
quiz.explanation: Lifting it early lets oxygen back in, and hot oil can reignite.

situations: It's {time}. {name} is frying snacks when the oil in the pan suddenly catches fire. Flames reach up toward the chimney hood, and {relation} runs in with a mug of water.
{name} is helping make pakoras {at}. The oil overheats and bursts into flames. Someone shouts 'Get water!'
scenario.question: What should {name} do, right now?
scenario.bubble: Should I throw water?!

rubric.point: Stop anyone from using water
rubric.note: Water on burning oil causes a fireball.

rubric.point: Turn off the heat source
rubric.note: Switching off the gas stops the fire getting fuel.

rubric.point: Cover the pan with a metal lid or damp cloth
rubric.note: Covering it cuts off oxygen. The fastest way to put out a small oil fire.

rubric.point: Get out and call for help if it spreads
rubric.note: Leave, close the door, call 101 (fire) or 112.

cards.title: Getting out of a building fire
facts: Smoke rises, so the cleanest air is near the floor.
Lifts can stop or open onto a smoky floor during a fire.
Closed doors slow down fire and smoke.
do: Shout 'Fire!' to warn others
Use the stairs, never the lift
Stay low under smoke
Feel doors with the back of your hand before opening
Close doors behind you
Go to the assembly point and stay there
Call 101 or 112 once you're safe
dont: Don't use the lift
Don't stop to collect belongings
Never go back inside

myths.statement: If there's a fire in your building, take the lift. It's the fastest way out.
myths.truth: Lifts can stop working or open onto a smoky floor. Always use the stairs.

myths.statement: In a smoky room, crawling low helps you breathe cleaner air.
myths.truth: Smoke and heat rise, so the air near the floor is cleaner.

quiz.q: The fire alarm rings in your apartment building. How do you go down?
options: Go up to the roof first
quiz.explanation: Stairs are the safe way out. Lifts can fail in a fire.

quiz.q: Before opening a door during a fire, you should…
options: Feel it with the back of your hand
quiz.explanation: A hot door means fire on the other side. Use another way out.

situations: {name} is {at}, on the 6th floor, when the fire alarm goes off and the corridor starts filling with grey smoke. {relation} heads straight for the lift.
It's {time}. {name} smells smoke and hears the alarm {at}. The door to the stairwell is closed, and people are shouting.
scenario.question: What should {name} do to get out safely?
scenario.bubble: Let's take the lift!

rubric.point: Use the stairs, not the lift
rubric.note: Lifts can stop or open onto a smoky floor.

rubric.point: Stay low under the smoke
rubric.note: Cleaner air is near the floor.

rubric.point: Check doors for heat and close doors behind
rubric.note: Hot door = fire behind it. Closed doors slow the fire.

rubric.point: Get out, go to the assembly point, call 101/112

cards.reviewNote: Drafted from widely published guidance. Needs expert review before launch.

cards.title: Electrical fires and sockets
facts: Water conducts electricity, so it can cause electric shock on an electrical fire.
Overloaded sockets and damaged wires are a common cause of home fires.
Dry powder (ABC) or CO2 extinguishers are suitable for electrical fires.
do: Switch off power at the main switch if it's safe
Tell an adult immediately
Get out and call 101 or 112 if it grows
Report burning smells and sparking sockets
dont: Never throw water on an electrical fire
Don't plug many heavy appliances into one socket
Don't touch a sparking socket

myths.statement: It's fine to use water on a burning TV as long as you're quick.
myths.truth: Water conducts electricity. Cut the power first and use the right extinguisher, or get out.

quiz.q: A phone charger starts sparking and smoking. First step?
options: Switch off the power if safe and tell an adult
Pull the wire with wet hands
quiz.explanation: Cutting the power removes the danger. Never use water.

situations: {name} is studying {at} when the extension board under the desk starts sparking and a thin line of smoke rises. {relation} grabs a bottle of water.
scenario.question: What should {name} do?
scenario.bubble: Splash water on it!

rubric.point: Don't use water on an electrical fire
Switch off power at the main switch if safe
Tell an adult and get out / call 101 or 112 if it grows
Use a suitable extinguisher only if trained
rubric.note: ABC dry powder or CO2 are suitable for electrical fires.

cards.reviewNote: Drafted from widely published guidance. Needs expert review before launch.

cards.title: Diyas and firecrackers
facts: Most festival burns happen to hands, face and eyes.
Synthetic clothes can melt onto skin; cotton is safer.
A cracker that didn't go off can still explode later.
do: Only use crackers with an adult watching
Keep a bucket of water and sand nearby
Light at arm's length and step back
Wear cotton clothes and closed shoes
Keep diyas away from curtains and loose clothes
dont: Never relight a cracker that didn't go off
Don't hold crackers in your hand
Don't burst crackers indoors or near vehicles

myths.statement: If a cracker doesn't go off, it's safe to walk up and light it again.
myths.truth: A dud can explode without warning. Wait, then soak it in water.

quiz.q: What should be kept nearby when bursting crackers?
options: A bucket of water and sand
quiz.explanation: Water and sand help with small fires and duds.

situations: It's Diwali night. {At}, a cracker {name} lit doesn't go off. {relation} says 'Go check it and light it again!'
scenario.question: What should {name} do?
scenario.bubble: Just light it again!

rubric.point: Don't go near or relight the dud
Wait, then soak it in a bucket of water
Make sure an adult is supervising

cards.reviewNote: Drafted from widely published guidance. Needs expert review before launch.

cards.title: LPG cylinder leak smell in kitchen
facts: LPG has ethyl mercaptan added so even tiny leaks smell like rotten eggs.
Flipping an electric switch creates a microscopic spark that can ignite accumulated gas.
do: Open all doors and windows to disperse the gas
Turn off cylinder regulator if safe
Leave the house and call 1906 / 112 from outside
dont: Never turn electrical switches on or off
Never light matches or candles

myths.statement: Turning on an exhaust fan helps clear LPG gas quickly.
myths.truth: Exhaust switches create electrical sparks that ignite gas. Open windows manually.

quiz.q: You smell LPG gas in the kitchen. What is the safest first action?
options: Open windows and do not touch switches
Light a match to find the leak
quiz.explanation: Electrical switches cause sparks. Open windows naturally and never touch switches.

situations: At {time}, {name} walks into the kitchen at {at} and smells strong LPG gas near the stove.
scenario.question: What should {name} do right now?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Do not touch electrical switches or flames
Open doors and windows for ventilation
rubric.note: Lets heavy LPG gas disperse outside.

rubric.point: Turn off regulator and evacuate outside
rubric.note: Cuts fuel and keeps family safe.

cards.title: Clothes catch fire: Stop, Drop and Roll
facts: Running feeds oxygen to burning clothes, making flames spread much faster.
Rolling on the ground smothers flames by depriving them of air.
do: Stop moving immediately without running
Drop to the ground and cover face with hands
Roll back and forth until flames extinguish
dont: Never run when clothes are burning
Don't peel off clothes stuck to burned skin

myths.statement: If clothes catch fire, running to a bathroom is the best response.
myths.truth: Running creates air currents that fan the flames. Stop, Drop and Roll immediately.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do if your clothes catch fire?
options: Stop, drop to the ground, and roll
Fan the flames with a towel
quiz.explanation: Stop, Drop, and Roll cuts off oxygen and extinguishes flames quickly.

situations: During a festival at {at}, a spark touches {name}'s sleeve and the fabric catches fire.
scenario.question: What must {name} do immediately?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Stop moving immediately without running
Drop to ground and protect face
Roll back and forth to smother fire

cards.title: Operating a fire extinguisher: PASS method
facts: Fire extinguishers are only meant for small incipient fires smaller than a dustbin.
PASS stands for Pull pin, Aim low, Squeeze handle, Sweep side-to-side.
do: Ensure you have a clear escape exit behind you
Pull the pin, aim at the base of the fire
Squeeze handle and sweep side to side
dont: Never aim at the top flames
Never corner yourself without an exit

myths.statement: You should aim the fire extinguisher directly at the top of the flames.
myths.truth: Aiming at flames wastes the agent. Aim low at the fuel base.

quiz.q: What does the 'A' in the PASS technique stand for?
quiz.explanation: A stands for Aim low at the base of the fire where fuel is burning.

situations: In the school lab at {at}, a waste basket catches fire. An adult brings an extinguisher.
scenario.question: How should the extinguisher be operated?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Pull the safety pin
Aim low at the base of the fire
Squeeze handle and sweep side to side

cards.title: Testing closed doors during a fire
facts: Opening a hot door can cause a backdraft or let toxic smoke rush in.
Use the back of your hand to feel the door and knob so you don't burn your palm.
do: Feel door and handle with the back of your hand
If warm, keep closed and seek another exit
Seal door cracks with cloth if trapped
dont: Never open a warm or hot door
Never touch door with open palm

myths.statement: Peeking open a hot door slightly is safe to check the fire.
myths.truth: Opening even a crack allows superheated smoke and gas to flash over into the room.

quiz.q: How should you test a closed room door during a fire alarm?
options: Feel door and knob with back of hand
quiz.explanation: Touch with back of hand. If warm, keep closed to block flames.

situations: A fire alarm sounds at {at}. {name} reaches the bedroom door to exit into the hallway.
scenario.question: What must {name} do before opening the door?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Touch door and knob with back of hand
rubric.note: Detects heat safely without burning palm.

rubric.point: Keep door shut if warm or hot
Use alternate window escape or signal for rescue

cards.title: Smoke inhalation and crawling low
facts: Smoke and toxic gases rise; cleaner, cooler air remains 30 to 60 cm above the floor.
Most fire casualties result from toxic smoke inhalation rather than direct burns.
do: Drop to hands and knees immediately
Crawl low under smoke toward the nearest exit
Cover nose and mouth with a damp cloth if possible
dont: Never walk upright through thick smoke
Don't stop to collect belongings

myths.statement: Holding your breath while walking tall lets you escape smoke safely.
myths.truth: One breath of toxic smoke can cause unconsciousness. Stay low where air is clean.

quiz.q: Where is the cleanest air located in a smoke-filled room?
quiz.explanation: Heat and smoke rise, leaving a layer of breathable air near the floor.

situations: Thick dark smoke begins filling the hallway at {at} during an emergency.
scenario.question: How should {name} move through the smoke to escape?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Drop down and crawl low on hands and knees
Cover nose and mouth with a cloth
Head continuously toward the nearest exit

sources.name: Indian Red Cross Fire First Aid

cards.title: Surviving trapped in a room during fire
facts: Sealing gaps prevents smoke from suffocating occupants trapped inside.
Hanging a bright cloth from a window signals firefighters to your location.
do: Close door tightly and seal bottom cracks with wet cloth
Open window slightly for fresh air if no smoke outside
Call 112 / 101 and wave bright cloth from window
dont: Never jump from high floors
Never break windows if smoke is outside

myths.statement: Breaking bedroom windows is always the best move if trapped by fire.
myths.truth: If outside has smoke or flames, breaking glass draws fire inside. Signal without breaking.

quiz.q: If trapped in a room by hallway fire, what should you seal door cracks with?
quiz.explanation: Wet towels or cloth block smoke from penetrating under the door.

situations: Flames in the corridor block {name}'s exit from the room at {at}.
scenario.question: What should {name} do to stay safe until rescued?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Close door and seal cracks with wet cloth
Call 112 / 101 and report exact room location
Signal from the window with a cloth or flashlight

cards.title: School fire drills and assembly points
facts: Panic and stampedes cause more injuries during evacuations than flames.
School assembly grounds ensure teachers can conduct headcount roll calls.
do: Follow teacher instructions and walk briskly without pushing
Leave heavy backpacks and bags behind
Assemble quietly at the designated muster ground for roll call
dont: Never run, push or scream during evacuation
Never return inside for bags, phones or homework

myths.statement: During a fire alarm, grabbing your school bag is fine if it takes 5 seconds.
myths.truth: Every second counts in fire evacuation. Leave bags; save lives.

quiz.q: What is the most important rule when leaving the classroom during a fire drill?
options: Run as fast as you can
Walk calmly in line without pushing
quiz.explanation: Orderly walking prevents fatal stairwell crushes and stampedes.

situations: The fire alarm rings loudly across the school building at {at}.
scenario.question: How should {name} and classmates exit the classroom?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Leave all bags and personal items behind
Walk calmly in single file without running or shoving
Assemble at the designated outdoor sports ground for headcount

sources.name: Ministry of Education School Safety Manual

cards.title: Matches and lighters away from young kids
facts: Young children perceive lighters and matchsticks as toys rather than hazards.
Most residential fires sparked by children occur in bedrooms and closets.
do: Store matches, lighters, and pooja materials in high locked cupboards
Teach younger siblings that fire tools are adults-only tools
Hand any stray matchbox found on floor to an adult immediately
dont: Never leave lighters on low coffee tables or beds
Never let children play with diyas or sparklers

myths.statement: Giving an empty lighter to a toddler as a toy is harmless.
myths.truth: Empty lighters still spark and teach dangerous mimicking habits.

quiz.q: Where should matchboxes and lighters always be stored at home?
options: In a high, locked cabinet out of reach of children
quiz.explanation: Storing out of children's reach prevents accidental house fires.

situations: At home at {at}, {name} sees their 4-year-old cousin playing with a lighter on the sofa.
scenario.question: What should {name} do right away?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Gently take the lighter away from the child
Hand it to a parent or adult immediately
Store it in a high secure cabinet

cards.title: Mosquito coils, candles, and agarbatti
facts: A glowing mosquito coil tip reaches over 500°C and can ignite paper or curtains easily.
Leaving candles or coils burning while asleep causes nocturnal house fires.
do: Keep coils on sturdy metal stands inside deep metal plates
Keep candles at least 1 meter away from curtains, beds, and books
Extinguish all burning coils and candles before going to sleep
dont: Never place coils directly on cardboard, plastic or carpets
Never leave lit candles unattended in empty rooms

myths.statement: Mosquito coils burn at low temperatures and cannot ignite fabric.
myths.truth: Coil embers burn at 500°C and easily set mattresses and bedsheets on fire.

quiz.q: What should always be placed under a mosquito coil stand?
options: A wide metal or ceramic plate
quiz.explanation: Metal or ceramic plates catch falling hot ash safely without burning.

situations: At bedtime at {at}, {name} notices an agarbatti burning right beside blowing window curtains.
scenario.question: What action should {name} take?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Move the incense far away from curtains and fabric
Place on heatproof ceramic or metal holder
Extinguish if nobody is in the room or before sleeping

cards.title: Socket overloading and extension board safety
facts: Plugging multiple heating appliances into one strip exceeds wire amp ratings.
Overloaded circuits heat up inside walls, causing hidden attic and wall fires.
do: Plug high-power devices (heaters, irons, geysers) directly into dedicated wall sockets
Check extension cords for frayed insulation or melting smells
Unplug chargers and boards when not in active use
dont: Never plug multiple extension boards into each other (daisy chaining)
Never run power cords under rugs or doorways

myths.statement: You can plug an iron, microwave, and kettle into one strip if it has enough holes.
myths.truth: Current draw will exceed the cord's rating, melting plastic and causing fires.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to plug a room heater into a cheap power strip?
options: Heaters draw heavy current that can melt the strip and ignite fire
quiz.explanation: High-wattage appliances draw heavy currents that overheat thin extension wires.

situations: In the study room at {at}, {name} sees an iron, room heater, and laptop plugged into a single cheap multi-plug adapter that feels hot.
scenario.question: What should {name} do?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Switch off and unplug high-draw appliances immediately
rubric.note: Stops current overload before melting occurs.

rubric.point: Do not touch burning or melted plastic with bare hands
Inform parents and connect heater directly to 15A wall socket

cards.title: Overheating phone and power bank charging
facts: Lithium-ion batteries can enter thermal runaway if punctured, crushed or overheated.
Charging phones under pillows traps heat, preventing natural dissipation.
do: Charge phones on hard, flat, ventilated surfaces like tables
Stop using and safely dispose of any swollen or bulging battery
Unplug chargers once the device reaches full charge
dont: Never charge phones under pillows or on mattresses overnight
Never use cheap uncertified replacement chargers

myths.statement: Charging your phone under a soft pillow is completely safe.
myths.truth: Pillows trap charging heat, leading to battery swelling and explosion.

quiz.q: What should you do if your power bank feels unusually hot and swollen?
options: Stop using and charging it immediately; move to fire-safe area
quiz.explanation: Swollen batteries can burst into flame. Discontinue use immediately.

situations: At night at {at}, {name} finds their phone charging tucked under their sleeping pillow, feeling burning hot.
scenario.question: What is the safest move for {name}?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Unplug the charger from the wall socket
Move phone off bed onto a hard, non-flammable desk
rubric.note: Allows phone to dissipate heat safely.

rubric.point: Never sleep with phone under pillow or bedding

cards.title: Vehicle fire evacuation in cars and buses
facts: Vehicle fires spread rapidly due to fuel, oil, upholstery, and electrical wires.
Smoke and toxic fumes fill a closed vehicle cabin in under 60 seconds.
do: Alert driver and passengers calmly to pull over safely
Evacuate everyone immediately and move at least 30 meters away
Call 112 / 101 from a safe distance outside
dont: Never return inside a burning car for bags or valuables
Never stand downwind of vehicle smoke

myths.statement: If a car catches fire, you should open the bonnet wide to blow it out.
myths.truth: Opening the bonnet lets in massive oxygen, creating an immediate fireball.

quiz.q: If smoke begins billowing from a school bus bonnet, what should students do?
options: Evacuate calmly through doors and move 30 meters away
quiz.explanation: Evacuate quickly and maintain safe standoff distance in case of fuel tank rupture.

situations: While traveling in a vehicle at {at}, {name} notices acrid electrical smoke pouring from under the dashboard.
scenario.question: What should {name} and passengers do?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Instruct driver to stop vehicle and turn off ignition
rubric.note: Cuts fuel pump and electrical flow.

rubric.point: Evacuate all passengers immediately without gathering luggage
rubric.note: Saves lives before toxic fumes accumulate.

rubric.point: Move at least 30 meters upwind and call 112
rubric.note: Keeps safe distance from fuel explosion.

sources.name: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways

cards.title: Bonfire and garden leaf burning safety
facts: Burning dry leaves releases toxic fine particulate matter and risks runaway fires.
Unattended bonfires can be reignited hours later by sudden wind gusts.
do: Clear a 3-meter safety ring of bare dirt around any fire pit
Keep a bucket of water or sand right next to the campfire
Drown the coals completely with water and stir until cold before leaving
dont: Never burn plastic, rubber or treated wood
Never walk away from an active campfire

myths.statement: If a campfire stops showing flames, it is safe to leave without water.
myths.truth: Deep embers retain heat for over 24 hours. Drown with water until cool to touch.

quiz.q: How do you ensure a campfire is completely extinguished before leaving?
options: Pour water, stir ashes, and feel that coals are cold
quiz.explanation: Drown, stir, and check temperature to ensure no hidden hot embers remain.

situations: After an outdoor camping activity at {at}, the campfire is smoking but flames are gone.
scenario.question: How should {name} and team properly extinguish the pit?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Drench all embers thoroughly with water
Stir the ashes with a stick and add more water
Confirm ashes are completely cold to the touch

sources.name: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

cards.title: Grass and forest fire on hiking trails
facts: Wildfires move uphill much faster than downhill because rising heat pre-warms slope vegetation.
Shifting wind directions can rapidly trap hikers in steep valleys.
do: Move downhill and downwind toward natural fire breaks like rivers or wide roads
Stay in cleared areas with sparse vegetation
Call forest helpline or 112 with exact trail landmarks
dont: Never try to outrun a fire heading uphill
Never hide inside narrow ravines or caves

myths.statement: When escaping a forest fire on a mountain, running uphill is safer.
myths.truth: Flames race uphill twice as fast as downhill. Always escape downhill and sideways.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to run uphill when escaping a forest fire?
options: Heat and flames travel uphill significantly faster
quiz.explanation: Rising convective heat pre-heats uphill brush, causing fires to explode upward.

situations: While on a hillside trek at {at}, {name} spots a fast-moving brush fire advancing up the slope.
scenario.question: Which direction should {name} evacuate?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Move downhill and sideways toward cleared terrain
rubric.note: Fire races uphill; downhill provides escape time.

rubric.point: Avoid narrow ravines and dense dry thickets
rubric.note: Ravines act as natural chimneys for fire.

rubric.point: Alert trek leader and call emergency services 112

sources.name: Forest Survey of India Wildfire Guidelines

cards.title: Creating a home fire escape plan
facts: Families have as little as two minutes to escape safely once a smoke alarm sounds.
Having a designated meeting spot outside ensures everyone is accounted for quickly.
do: Map two exit paths (door and window) from every bedroom
Designate a fixed meeting spot outside (e.g. big tree or park gate)
Practise the escape drill with family twice a year
dont: Never use lifts or elevators during any building fire
Never search for pets or toys during evacuation

myths.statement: During a house fire, everyone should gather in the living room first.
myths.truth: Gathering indoors risks getting trapped. Everyone must escape outside to the meeting spot.

quiz.q: What is the most crucial part of a family fire escape plan?
options: Having two ways out of every room and a fixed outdoor meeting point
quiz.explanation: Two exits and an outside meeting spot prevent people being trapped inside.

situations: {name}'s family at {at} is creating their yearly home fire safety plan.
scenario.question: What key elements must {name} include in the family plan?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Identify two exit routes from every room
rubric.note: Ensures backup if main door is blocked.

rubric.point: Pick a fixed outdoor meeting spot outside the building
Never take elevators; always take stairways
rubric.note: Prevents getting trapped in elevator shafts.

cards.title: Safety rules for re-entering a fire-affected building
facts: Burned structures suffer hidden beam weaknesses, gas pockets, and toxic ash.
Smoldering embers inside wall cavities can reignite hours after flames are doused.
do: Wait until the fire department officially declares the structure safe
Wear sturdy closed shoes and a particulate mask when re-entering
Have an electrician inspect house wiring before restoring power
dont: Never enter a burned building without fire officer permission
Never use damaged switches or gas valves

myths.statement: Once flames are out, families can move back into the house immediately.
myths.truth: Structural weakness, carbon monoxide, and damaged wiring present deadly post-fire hazards.

quiz.q: Who must grant permission before anyone re-enters a house after a fire?
options: The Fire Department or municipal safety engineer
quiz.explanation: Only fire officials can verify structural stability and absence of toxic gases.

situations: A fire at {at} was extinguished by firefighters an hour ago. {name}'s friend wants to run inside to grab their laptop.
scenario.question: What should {name} advise?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Do not enter until fire officers declare it safe
Beware of structural collapse and live fallen wires
Do not flip electrical mains back on without inspection
